<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">I-ViT: Integer-only Quantization for Efficient Vision Transformer Inference</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Zhikai Li
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>School of Artificial Intelligence, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_email"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Email: </span><a href="mailto:lizhikai2020@ia.ac.cn">lizhikai2020@ia.ac.cn</a>
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Qingyi Gu
</span><span id="id1" class="ltx_note ltx_note_frontmatter ltx_thanks_correspondence ltx_role_thanks"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">thanks: </span>Corresponding author.</span></span></span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_email"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Email: </span><a href="mailto:qingyi.gu@ia.ac.cn">qingyi.gu@ia.ac.cn</a>
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Vision Transformers (ViTs) have achieved state-of-the-art performance on various computer vision applications. However, these models have considerable storage and computational overheads, making their deployment and efficient inference on edge devices challenging. Quantization is a promising approach to reducing model complexity, and the dyadic arithmetic pipeline can allow the quantized models to perform efficient integer-only inference. Unfortunately, dyadic arithmetic is based on the homogeneity condition in convolutional neural networks, which is not applicable to the non-linear components in ViTs, making integer-only inference of ViTs an open issue. In this paper, we propose I-ViT, an integer-only quantization scheme for ViTs, to enable ViTs to perform the entire computational graph of inference with integer arithmetic and bit-shifting, and without any floating-point arithmetic. In I-ViT, linear operations (e.g., MatMul and Dense) follow the integer-only pipeline with dyadic arithmetic, and non-linear operations (e.g., Softmax, GELU, and LayerNorm) are approximated by the proposed light-weight integer-only arithmetic methods. More specifically, I-ViT applies the proposed Shiftmax and ShiftGELU, which are designed to use integer bit-shifting to approximate the corresponding floating-point operations. We evaluate I-ViT on various benchmark models and the results show that integer-only INT8 quantization achieves comparable (or even slightly higher) accuracy to the full-precision (FP) baseline. Furthermore, we utilize TVM for practical hardware deployment on the GPU’s integer arithmetic units, achieving 3.72<math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>4.11<math id="abstract1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> inference speedup compared to the FP model. Code of both Pytorch and TVM is released at <a href="https://github.com/zkkli/I-ViT" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/zkkli/I-ViT</a>.</p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_text"></span></p>
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Vision Transformers (ViTs) have recently achieved great success on a variety of computer vision tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>, <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>, <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite>. Nevertheless, as compared to convolutional neural networks (CNNs), ViTs suffer from higher memory footprints, computational overheads, and power consumption, hindering their deployment and real-time inference on resource-constrained edge devices <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>, <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>, <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>, <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>]</cite>. Thus, compression approaches for ViTs are being widely researched.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<figure id="S1.F1.sf1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2207.01405v4/1-1.svg" id="S1.F1.sf1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:288/274;" width="288" height="274"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F1.sf1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">(a)</span> </span><span id="S1.F1.sf1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">FasterTransformer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>]</cite></span></figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<figure id="S1.F1.sf2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><img src="2207.01405v4/1-2.png" id="S1.F1.sf2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:288/275;" width="288" height="275" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F1.sf2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">(b)</span> </span><span id="S1.F1.sf2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">I-ViT (ours)</span></figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>Computation flows of Softmax, GELU, and LayerNorm in FasterTransformer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>]</cite> and our proposed I-ViT. I-ViT realizes the entire computational graph with integer-only arithmetic, which is more promising and practical for low-cost model deployment and efficient inference.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Model quantization, which reduces the representation precision of weight/activation parameters, is an effective and hardware-friendly way to improve model efficiency <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>, <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>, <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>, <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite>.
With the quantized low-precision parameters, previous work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite> presents the dyadic arithmetic pipeline to realize integer-only inference, where the quantization scaling factors are collapsed into the integer multiplication and bit-shifting in the requantization process. This can enable the quantized models to fully benefit from the fast and efficient low-precision integer arithmetic units and thus provides promising speedup effects <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>, <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">44</a>]</cite>. For instance, the edge processor core in ARM Cortex-M family only support the deployment of the integer-only kernels; the recent Turing Tensor Cores in GPU server class also add support for integer logical units, and their high throughput capability enables notably lower latency compared to floating-point arithmetic.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">However, the above integer-only pipeline is designed for CNNs and works under the homogeneity condition, making it only applicable to linear (<math id="S1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>e</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e</annotation></semantics></math>.<math id="S1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math>., Dense) or piecewise linear (<math id="S1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>e</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e</annotation></semantics></math>.<math id="S1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math>., ReLU) operations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>, <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">44</a>]</cite>. Therefore, the non-linear operations (<math id="S1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>e</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e</annotation></semantics></math>.<math id="S1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math>., Softmax, GELU, and LayerNorm) in ViTs cannot naively follow it. To cope with this problem, a brute-force scheme is to simply leave the non-linear operations as dequantized floating-point arithmetic, such as FasterTransformer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>]</cite> shown in Figure <a href="#S1.F1.sf2" title="In Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ I-ViT: Integer-only Quantization for Efficient Vision Transformer Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1(b)</span></a>(a). Unfortunately, this scheme makes them tolerate the inefficiency of floating-point arithmetic units, and the cut of the computational graph also introduces communication costs between integer and floating-point units, which severely limits the speedup of inference. In addition, low-cost integer-only hardware cannot meet mixed-precision computing requirements, hence one has to design heterogeneous chips by adding floating-point arithmetic units, which definitely increases the budget for model deployment.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Consequently, integer-only arithmetic for non-linear operations is significant for low-cost deployment and efficient inference. To this end, several works have attempted on language Transformer models. Fully-8bit <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>]</cite> employs L1 LayerNorm to replace the non-linear arithmetic of standard deviation, and I-BERT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite> proposes integer polynomial approximations for the non-linear operations. However, such approaches are inefficient and fail to fully exploit the benefits of hardware logic. Moreover, they are developed for language models, making it infeasible to properly transfer to ViTs due to differences in data distribution.
For ViTs, FQ-ViT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>]</cite> preliminarily explores the feasibility of integer arithmetic for part of the operations (<math id="S1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>e</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e</annotation></semantics></math>.<math id="S1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math>., Softmax), but it is simply built on I-BERT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite> and ignores the notable GELU operation, leaving a huge gap between it and integer-only inference.
As a result, <em id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">how to accurately perform the non-linear operations of ViTs with efficient integer-only arithmetic</em> remains an open issue.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, we propose I-ViT, which quantizes the entire computational graph to fill the research gap of integer-only quantization for ViTs.
Specifically, linear operations follow the dyadic arithmetic pipeline; and non-linear operations are approximated without accuracy drop by novel light-weight integer-only arithmetic methods, where Shiftmax and ShiftGELU perform most arithmetic with bit-shifting that can be efficiently executed with simple shifters in hardware logic <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>]</cite>, and I-LayerNorm calculates the square root with integer iterations instead.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">The main contributions are summarized as follows:</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We propose I-ViT, which fully quantizes the computational graph of ViTs and allows performing the entire inference with integer arithmetic and bit-shifting, without any floating-point operations. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work on integer-only quantization for ViTs.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We propose novel light-weight integer approximations for non-linear operations (as shown in Figure <a href="#S1.F1.sf2" title="In Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ I-ViT: Integer-only Quantization for Efficient Vision Transformer Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1(b)</span></a>(b)), in particular, Shiftmax and ShiftGELU use integer bit-shifting to accomplish most arithmetic, which fully benefit from the efficient hardware logic.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">I-ViT is evaluated on various models for the large-scale classification task, achieving compression with similar (or even slightly higher) accuracy. Moreover, we deploy I-ViT on an RTX 2080Ti GPU using TVM<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
                  <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
                  
                  
                  
                <a href="https://github.com/apache/tvm" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/apache/tvm</a></span></span></span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite>, which accelerates the integer-only inference of ViTs with Turing Tensor Cores, achieving a 3.72<math id="S1.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>4.11<math id="S1.I1.i3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> speedup over the FP model (as shown in Figure <a href="#S1.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ I-ViT: Integer-only Quantization for Efficient Vision Transformer Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>).</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2207.01405v4/3.png" id="S1.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/341;" width="548" height="341" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>Accuracy-speed curves of I-ViT and the FP baseline on DeiT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite> and Swin <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>]</cite>. Accuracy is evaluated on ImageNet dataset, and speed is obtained from the latency on an RTX 2080Ti GPU (batch=8). As we can see, I-ViT provides significant accelerations (3.72<math id="S1.F2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>4.11<math id="S1.F2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>) while achieving similar (or even slightly higher) accuracy.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Works</h2>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Vision Transformers</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Thanks to the global receptive fields captured by the attention mechanism, ViTs have shown superior performance on various computer vision tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>, <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">42</a>, <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite>. ViT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite> is the first effort to apply transformer-based models to vision applications and achieves high accuracy than CNNs on the classification task.
DeiT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite> introduces an efficient teacher-student strategy via adding a distillation token, reducing the time and data cost in the training phase.
Swin <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>]</cite> presents shifted window attentions at various scales, which boosts the performance of ViTs.
Furthermore, ViTs have also been applied to more complexed vision applications, such as object detection <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>, <a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">51</a>]</cite>, semantic segmentation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>]</cite>, and video recognition <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Despite the promising performance, ViTs’ complicated architectures with large memory footprints and computational overheads is intolerable in real-world applications <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>, <a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>, <a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">47</a>, <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite>, especially in time/resource-constrained scenarios. Thus, the compression approaches for ViTs are necessary for practical deployments.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Model Quantization</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Model quantization, which converts the floating-point parameters to low-precision values, is a prevalent solution to compressing models in a hardware-friendly manner <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>, <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>, <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>, <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>]</cite>.
Most previous works are designed to quantize CNNs.
DoReFa <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>]</cite> and LQ-Net <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">46</a>]</cite> approximate the gradient propagation in quantization-aware training by straight-through estimator (STE) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite>.
PACT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite> and LSQ <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>, <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite> treat the activation clipping value/step size as trainable parameters and achieve promising results on low-bit quantization.
In addition, several notable works adopt more advanced quantization strategies, including non-uniform quantization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>]</cite>, channel-wise quantization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite>, and mixed-precision quantization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>, <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>]</cite> etc.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Recently, several quantization methods oriented to ViTs’ unique structures are proposed.
Ranking loss <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>]</cite> is presented to maintain the correct relative order of the quantized attention map.
Q-ViT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>]</cite> proposes differentiable quantization for ViTs, taking the quantization bit-widths and scales as learnable parameters.
PTQ4ViT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>]</cite> proposes twin uniform quantization and uses a Hessian guided metric to evaluate different scaling factors.
FQ-ViT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>]</cite> introduces powers-of-two scale quantization and log-int quantization for LayerNorm and Softmax, respectively.
RepQ-ViT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite> decouples the quantization and inference processes to address the extreme distributions of LayerNorm and Softmax activations.
PSAQ-ViT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>, <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>]</cite> pushes the quantization of ViTs to data-free scenarios based on patch similarity.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">However, in the above approaches, all or part of the operations are performed with dequantized floating-point parameters during inference, which fails to fully use efficient low-precision arithmetic units and thus provides unsatisfactory model acceleration.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3 </span>Integer-only quantization</h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Integer-only quantization, which eliminates dequantization and enables the entire inference to be performed with integer-only arithmetic, can potentially address the above challenges. Dyadic arithmetic is proposed to perform the integer-only pipeline for CNNs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>, <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">44</a>]</cite>, however, it is designed for linear and piecewise linear operations based on the homogeneity condition, and thus is not applicable to non-linear operations in ViTs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Therefore, several studies are interested in how to achieve integer arithmetic for non-linear operations in language Transformer models. Fully-8bit <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>]</cite> introduces L1 LayerNorm, which avoids the non-linearity of solving for the square root when calculating the standard deviation.
I-BERT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite> focuses on integer polynomial approximations for the non-linear operations, including Softmax, GELU, and LayerNorm.
It is worth noting that although these three component approximations can potentially enable integer-only inference of ViTs (partly verified by FQ-ViT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>]</cite>), the computation of high-order polynomials is inefficient in inference, and they are developed for language models that do not fit the data distribution of ViTs, leading to mismatched approximations.
In addition, various approximation methods that hold floating-point arithmetic are presented <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>, <a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">50</a>]</cite>; while they lower certain computational costs, they cannot meet the demands of integer arithmetic. As a result, integer-only quantization for ViTs remains a research gap.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2207.01405v4/2.png" id="S2.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:685/592;" width="685" height="592" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span>Overview of the proposed I-ViT. The entire computational graph is performed with integer-only arithmetic, where linear MatMul and Dense operations follow the dyadic arithmetic pipeline and the proposed Shiftmax, ShiftGELU, and I-LayerNorm accomplish the non-linear operations. Except for the labeled INT32, the remaining data streams are all INT8 precision.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Methodology</h2>

<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Overview</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The overview of the proposed integer-only quantization scheme for ViTs is illustrated as Figure <a href="#S2.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 2.3 Integer-only quantization ‣ 2 Related Works ‣ I-ViT: Integer-only Quantization for Efficient Vision Transformer Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>.
The main body of ViTs is a stack of blocks, and each block is divided into a multi-head self-attention (MSA) module and a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) module, which can be formulated as follows:</p>
<table id="S3.EGx1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.E1"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\hat{X}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>X</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\hat{X}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\text{MSA}(\text{LayerNorm}(X))+X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mtext>MSA</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext>LayerNorm</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\text{MSA}(\text{LayerNorm}(X))+X</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="S3.E2"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle Y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle Y</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\text{MLP}(\text{LayerNorm}(\hat{X}))+\hat{X}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mtext>MLP</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext>LayerNorm</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>X</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>X</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\text{MLP}(\text{LayerNorm}(\hat{X}))+\hat{X}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The MSA module learns inter-patch representations by calculating the global attention as follows:</p>
<table id="S3.EGx2" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.E3"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\text{MSA}(X)=\text{Concat}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mtext>MSA</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mtext>Concat</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\text{MSA}(X)=\text{Concat}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle(\text{Attn}_{1},\text{Attn}_{2},\ldots,\text{Attn}_{h})W^{O}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mtext>Attn</mtext><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mtext>Attn</mtext><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mtext>Attn</mtext><mi>h</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>W</mi><mi>O</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle(\text{Attn}_{1},\text{Attn}_{2},\ldots,\text{Attn}_{h})W^{O}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="S3.E4"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\text{where}\;\;\text{Attn}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>where</mtext><mo lspace="0.560em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mtext>Attn</mtext><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\text{where}\;\;\text{Attn}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\text{Softmax}\left(\frac{Q_{i}\cdot K_{i}^{T}}{\sqrt{d}}\right)V_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mtext>Softmax</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup></mrow><msqrt><mi>d</mi></msqrt></mfrac></mstyle><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\text{Softmax}\left(\frac{Q_{i}\cdot K_{i}^{T}}{\sqrt{d}}\right)V_{i}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math> is the number of the attention heads, <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> is the size of hidden features, and <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i=1,2,\cdots,h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋯</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i=1,2,\cdots,h</annotation></semantics></math>.
Here, <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> are query, key, and value, respectively, and they are obtained by linear projections, <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>.<math id="S3.SS1.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>e</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e</annotation></semantics></math>., <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q_{i}=XW_{i}^{Q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>Q</mi></msubsup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q_{i}=XW_{i}^{Q}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K_{i}=XW_{i}^{K}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>K</mi></msubsup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K_{i}=XW_{i}^{K}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V_{i}=XW_{i}^{V}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>V</mi></msubsup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V_{i}=XW_{i}^{V}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Then the MLP module employs two dense layers and a GELU activation function to learn high-dimensional representations as follows:</p>
<table id="S3.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{MLP}(\hat{X})=\text{GELU}(\hat{X}W_{1}+b_{1})W_{2}+b_{2}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mtext>MLP</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>X</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mtext>GELU</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>X</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{MLP}(\hat{X})=\text{GELU}(\hat{X}W_{1}+b_{1})W_{2}+b_{2}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we are interested in quantizing the entire computational graph of ViTs.
To facilitate TVM implementation, we apply the simplest <em id="S3.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">symmetric uniform quantization</em> as follows:</p>
<table id="S3.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I=\left\lfloor\frac{\text{clip}(R,-m,m)}{S}\right\rceil,\;\text{where}\,\,S=\frac{2m}{2^{k}-1}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>⌊</mo><mfrac><mrow><mtext>clip</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mi>S</mi></mfrac><mo>⌉</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.447em">,</mo><mrow><mrow><mtext>where</mtext><mo lspace="0.340em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>k</mi></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I=\left\lfloor\frac{\text{clip}(R,-m,m)}{S}\right\rceil,\;\text{where}\,\,S=\frac{2m}{2^{k}-1}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>I</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I</annotation></semantics></math> denote the floating-point values and the quantized integer values, respectively, <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math> is the scaling factor of quantization, <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math> is the clipping value determined by the naive min-max method, <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> is the quantization bit-precision, and <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lfloor\cdot\rceil" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⌊</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">⌉</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lfloor\cdot\rceil</annotation></semantics></math> is the round operator.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">With the quantized integer values, to avoid dequantization and achieve integer-only inference, we apply the dyadic arithmetic pipeline for linear operations, as detailed in Section <a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Dyadic Arithmetic for Linear Operations ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ I-ViT: Integer-only Quantization for Efficient Vision Transformer Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>. Since the above pipeline is based on the homogeneity condition (<math id="S3.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>e</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e</annotation></semantics></math>.<math id="S3.SS1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math>., MatMul(<math id="S3.SS1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{Q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>Q</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{Q}</annotation></semantics></math>·<math id="S3.SS1.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I_{Q},S_{K}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>Q</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>K</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I_{Q},S_{K}</annotation></semantics></math>·<math id="S3.SS1.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I_{K}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I_{K}</annotation></semantics></math>)<math id="S3.SS1.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\equiv S_{Q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≡</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>Q</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\equiv S_{Q}</annotation></semantics></math>·<math id="S3.SS1.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{K}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{K}</annotation></semantics></math>·MatMul(<math id="S3.SS1.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I_{Q},I_{K}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>Q</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>K</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I_{Q},I_{K}</annotation></semantics></math>)), it is not applicable to the case of non-linearity (<math id="S3.SS1.p4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>e</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e</annotation></semantics></math>.<math id="S3.SS1.p4.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math>., Softmax(<math id="S3.SS1.p4.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{A}</annotation></semantics></math>·<math id="S3.SS1.p4.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I_{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I_{A}</annotation></semantics></math>)<math id="S3.SS1.p4.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\neq" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>≠</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\neq</annotation></semantics></math><math id="S3.SS1.p4.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{A}</annotation></semantics></math>·Softmax(<math id="S3.SS1.p4.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I_{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I_{A}</annotation></semantics></math>)). Thus, non-linear operations require accurate and efficient approximations by integer-only arithmetic. To this end, Shiftmax and ShiftGELU are proposed in this paper, which utilize efficient shifters in hardware logic to accomplish most arithmetic, and I-LayerNorm calculates the square root of the variance in an integer iterative manner. The above schemes are described in detail in Sections <a href="#S3.SS3" title="3.3 Integer-only Softmax: Shiftmax ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ I-ViT: Integer-only Quantization for Efficient Vision Transformer Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>-<a href="#S3.SS5" title="3.5 Integer-only LayerNorm: I-LayerNorm ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ I-ViT: Integer-only Quantization for Efficient Vision Transformer Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.5</span></a>, respectively.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Dyadic Arithmetic for Linear Operations</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The dyadic arithmetic pipeline, which uses integer bit-shifting to efficiently realize floating-point operations of scaling factors, allows linear operations to be performed with integer-only arithmetic.
Although it is designed for CNNs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>, <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">44</a>]</cite>, it can also be followed for linear operations in ViTs, including Conv in the embedding layer, and MatMul and Dense in the transformer layer.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Taking MatMul as an instance, when the inputs are <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q=(S_{Q},I_{Q})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>Q</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>Q</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q=(S_{Q},I_{Q})</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K=(S_{K},I_{K})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K=(S_{K},I_{K})</annotation></semantics></math>, the output is calculated as follows:</p>
<table id="S3.E7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A^{\prime}={S_{A}}^{\prime}\cdot{I_{A}}^{\prime}=S_{Q}\cdot S_{K}\cdot\left(I_{Q}*{I_{K}}^{T}\right)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>A</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mmultiscripts><mi>S</mi><mi>A</mi><mrow></mrow><mrow></mrow><mo>′</mo></mmultiscripts><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mmultiscripts><mi>I</mi><mi>A</mi><mrow></mrow><mrow></mrow><mo>′</mo></mmultiscripts></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>Q</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>Q</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">∗</mo><mmultiscripts><mi>I</mi><mi>K</mi><mrow></mrow><mrow></mrow><mi>T</mi></mmultiscripts></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A^{\prime}={S_{A}}^{\prime}\cdot{I_{A}}^{\prime}=S_{Q}\cdot S_{K}\cdot\left(I_{Q}*{I_{K}}^{T}\right)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(7)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{I_{A}}^{\prime}=I_{Q}*{I_{K}}^{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mmultiscripts><mi>I</mi><mi>A</mi><mrow></mrow><mrow></mrow><mo>′</mo></mmultiscripts><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>Q</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">∗</mo><mmultiscripts><mi>I</mi><mi>K</mi><mrow></mrow><mrow></mrow><mi>T</mi></mmultiscripts></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{I_{A}}^{\prime}=I_{Q}*{I_{K}}^{T}</annotation></semantics></math> performs integer-only arithmetic. Following the principle of practical hardware implementation (<math id="S3.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>e</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e</annotation></semantics></math>.<math id="S3.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math>., DP4A), when the inputs <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I_{Q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>Q</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I_{Q}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I_{K}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I_{K}</annotation></semantics></math> are INT8 types, the output <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{I_{A}}^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mmultiscripts><mi>I</mi><mi>A</mi><mrow></mrow><mrow></mrow><mo>′</mo></mmultiscripts><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{I_{A}}^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math> is INT32 type. Thus, we need to requantize <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{I_{A}}^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mmultiscripts><mi>I</mi><mi>A</mi><mrow></mrow><mrow></mrow><mo>′</mo></mmultiscripts><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{I_{A}}^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math> to INT8 type as the input for the next layer, which is calculated as follows:</p>
<table id="S3.E8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I_{A}=\left\lfloor\frac{{S_{A}}^{\prime}\cdot{I_{A}}^{\prime}}{S_{A}}\right\rceil=\left\lfloor\frac{S_{Q}\cdot S_{K}}{S_{A}}\cdot\left(I_{Q}*{I_{K}}^{T}\right)\right\rceil" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>⌊</mo><mfrac><mrow><mmultiscripts><mi>S</mi><mi>A</mi><mrow></mrow><mrow></mrow><mo>′</mo></mmultiscripts><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mmultiscripts><mi>I</mi><mi>A</mi><mrow></mrow><mrow></mrow><mo>′</mo></mmultiscripts></mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>A</mi></msub></mfrac><mo>⌉</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>⌊</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>Q</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>K</mi></msub></mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>A</mi></msub></mfrac><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>Q</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">∗</mo><mmultiscripts><mi>I</mi><mi>K</mi><mrow></mrow><mrow></mrow><mi>T</mi></mmultiscripts></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>⌉</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I_{A}=\left\lfloor\frac{{S_{A}}^{\prime}\cdot{I_{A}}^{\prime}}{S_{A}}\right\rceil=\left\lfloor\frac{S_{Q}\cdot S_{K}}{S_{A}}\cdot\left(I_{Q}*{I_{K}}^{T}\right)\right\rceil</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(8)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.3" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{A}</annotation></semantics></math> is the pre-calculated scaling factor of the output activation. Although the scaling factors remain floating-point values, their multiplication and division operations in Eq. <a href="#S3.E8" title="In 3.2 Dyadic Arithmetic for Linear Operations ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ I-ViT: Integer-only Quantization for Efficient Vision Transformer Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> can be avoided by converting the rescaling to a dyadic number (DN) as follows:</p>
<table id="S3.E9" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="DN\left(\frac{S_{Q}\cdot S_{K}}{S_{A}}\right)=\frac{b}{2^{c}}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>Q</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>K</mi></msub></mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>A</mi></msub></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>b</mi><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>c</mi></msup></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">DN\left(\frac{S_{Q}\cdot S_{K}}{S_{A}}\right)=\frac{b}{2^{c}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(9)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.4" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math> are both positive integer values. In this case, the rescaling can be efficiently accomplished by integer multiplication and bit-shifting. To summarize, the integer-only arithmetic pipeline of MatMul can be denoted as follows:</p>
<table id="S3.E10" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I_{A}=\left(b\cdot\left(I_{Q}*{I_{K}}^{T}\right)\right)\gg c" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>Q</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">∗</mo><mmultiscripts><mi>I</mi><mi>K</mi><mrow></mrow><mrow></mrow><mi>T</mi></mmultiscripts></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>≫</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I_{A}=\left(b\cdot\left(I_{Q}*{I_{K}}^{T}\right)\right)\gg c</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(10)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.5" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gg" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>≫</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gg</annotation></semantics></math> indicates right bit-shifting.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Integer-only Softmax: Shiftmax</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Softmax in ViTs translates the attention scores into probabilities, which acts on the hidden features and is calculated as follows:</p>
<table id="S3.E11" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E11.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{Softmax}(x_{i})=\frac{e^{x_{i}}}{\sum_{j}^{d}e^{x_{j}}}=\frac{e^{S_{x_{i}}\cdot I_{x_{i}}}}{\sum_{j}^{d}e^{S_{x_{j}}\cdot I_{x_{j}}}}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mtext>Softmax</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msup><mi>e</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></msup><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mi>j</mi><mi>d</mi></msubsup><msup><mi>e</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></msub></mrow></msup><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mi>j</mi><mi>d</mi></msubsup><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></msub></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{Softmax}(x_{i})=\frac{e^{x_{i}}}{\sum_{j}^{d}e^{x_{j}}}=\frac{e^{S_{x_{i}}\cdot I_{x_{i}}}}{\sum_{j}^{d}e^{S_{x_{j}}\cdot I_{x_{j}}}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(11)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i=1,2,\cdots,d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋯</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i=1,2,\cdots,d</annotation></semantics></math>.
Due to the non-linearity, Softmax cannot follow the dyadic arithmetic pipeline discussed above, and the exponential arithmetic in Eq. <a href="#S3.E11" title="In 3.3 Integer-only Softmax: Shiftmax ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ I-ViT: Integer-only Quantization for Efficient Vision Transformer Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> is typically unsupported by integer-only logic units <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>]</cite>. To address the above issues, we propose the approximation method Shiftmax, which can utilize simple hardware logic to achieve accurate and efficient integer-only arithmetic of Softmax. First, to smooth the data distribution and prevent overflow, we restrict the range of the exponential arithmetic as follows:</p>
<table id="S3.E12" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E12.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{Softmax}(x_{i})=\frac{e^{S_{\Delta_{i}}\cdot I_{\Delta_{i}}}}{\sum_{j}^{d}e^{S_{\Delta_{j}}\cdot I_{\Delta_{j}}}}=\frac{e^{S_{x_{i}}\cdot(I_{x_{i}}-I_{max})}}{\sum_{j}^{d}e^{S_{x_{j}}\cdot(I_{x_{j}}-I_{max})}}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mtext>Softmax</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></msub></mrow></msup><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mi>j</mi><mi>d</mi></msubsup><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></msub></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msup><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mi>j</mi><mi>d</mi></msubsup><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{Softmax}(x_{i})=\frac{e^{S_{\Delta_{i}}\cdot I_{\Delta_{i}}}}{\sum_{j}^{d}e^{S_{\Delta_{j}}\cdot I_{\Delta_{j}}}}=\frac{e^{S_{x_{i}}\cdot(I_{x_{i}}-I_{max})}}{\sum_{j}^{d}e^{S_{x_{j}}\cdot(I_{x_{j}}-I_{max})}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(12)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.3" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I_{max}=\max\{I_{x_{1}},I_{x_{2}},\cdots,I_{x_{d}}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>max</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></msub><mo>,</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋯</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I_{max}=\max\{I_{x_{1}},I_{x_{2}},\cdots,I_{x_{d}}\}</annotation></semantics></math>. Here, <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I_{\Delta_{i}}=I_{x_{i}}-I_{max}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I_{\Delta_{i}}=I_{x_{i}}-I_{max}</annotation></semantics></math> is a non-positive value and <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{\Delta_{i}}=S_{x_{i}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{\Delta_{i}}=S_{x_{i}}</annotation></semantics></math>, and we simplify them as <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I_{\Delta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>I</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I_{\Delta}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{\Delta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{\Delta}</annotation></semantics></math> in the following part for easier expression.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.2" class="ltx_p">Then, we are motivated to convert the base from <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>e</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math> to fully utilize the efficient shifters. Instead of a brute-force conversion, we perform an equivalent transformation using the base changing formula of the exponential function. Importantly, since <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\log_{2}e" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>log</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\log_{2}e</annotation></semantics></math> can be approximated by binary as <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(1.0111)_{b}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1.0111</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>b</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(1.0111)_{b}</annotation></semantics></math>, the floating-point multiplication with it can be achieved by integer shifting as follows:</p>
<table id="S3.E13" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="S3.E13X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E13X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle e^{S_{\Delta}\cdot I_{\Delta}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></msub></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle e^{S_{\Delta}\cdot I_{\Delta}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E13X.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=2^{S_{\Delta}\cdot(I_{\Delta}\cdot\log_{2}e)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mrow><msub><mi>log</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=2^{S_{\Delta}\cdot(I_{\Delta}\cdot\log_{2}e)}</annotation></semantics></math></td>

<td rowspan="2" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_right">(13)</span></td></tr>

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p3.3" class="ltx_p">The power term is denoted as <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{\Delta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{\Delta}</annotation></semantics></math>·<math id="S3.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I_{p}</annotation></semantics></math>, which is not ensured as an integer and cannot be directly used for shifting.
Thus, we decompose it into an integer part and a decimal part as follows:</p>
<table id="S3.E14" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E14.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2^{S_{\Delta}\cdot I_{p}}=2^{(-q)+S_{\Delta}\cdot(-r)}=2^{S_{\Delta}\cdot(-r)}\gg q" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msup><mo>≫</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2^{S_{\Delta}\cdot I_{p}}=2^{(-q)+S_{\Delta}\cdot(-r)}=2^{S_{\Delta}\cdot(-r)}\gg q</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(14)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.p3.4" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="S_{\Delta}\text{\textperiodcentered}(-r)\in(-1,0]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></msub><mtext>·</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em">−</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em">−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{\Delta}\text{\textperiodcentered}(-r)\in(-1,0]</annotation></semantics></math> is the decimal part, and <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> are both positive integer values.
For low-cost computation, we approximate <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2^{S_{\Delta}\cdot(-r)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2^{S_{\Delta}\cdot(-r)}</annotation></semantics></math> in range <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m7" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="(-1,0]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em">−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(-1,0]</annotation></semantics></math> by the linear function as follows:</p>
<table id="S3.E15" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="S3.E15X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

<p id="S3.SS3.p3.5" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I_{0}=\lfloor 1/S_{\Delta}\rceil" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⌊</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⌉</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I_{0}=\lfloor 1/S_{\Delta}\rceil</annotation></semantics></math>.
The above completes the approximation of the numerator in Eq. <a href="#S3.E12" title="In 3.3 Integer-only Softmax: Shiftmax ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ I-ViT: Integer-only Quantization for Efficient Vision Transformer Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a>, <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>.<math id="S3.SS3.p3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>e</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e</annotation></semantics></math>., <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{\Delta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{\Delta}</annotation></semantics></math>·<math id="S3.SS3.p3.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I_{exp}\approx e^{S_{\Delta}\cdot I_{\Delta}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msub><mo>≈</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I_{exp}\approx e^{S_{\Delta}\cdot I_{\Delta}}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{\Delta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{\Delta}</annotation></semantics></math> can be removed via fraction reduction since the scaling factor of the denominator obtained by summing is also <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{\Delta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{\Delta}</annotation></semantics></math>.
This turns Eq. <a href="#S3.E12" title="In 3.3 Integer-only Softmax: Shiftmax ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ I-ViT: Integer-only Quantization for Efficient Vision Transformer Inference" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a> into an integer division, which is calculated with the specified output bit-precision <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{out}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{out}</annotation></semantics></math> as follows:</p>
<table id="S3.E16" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="S3.E16X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>

<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E16X.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\frac{S_{\Delta}\cdot I_{exp_{i}}}{S_{\Delta}\cdot\sum_{j}^{d}I_{exp_{j}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.055em">⋅</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mi>j</mi><mi>d</mi></msubsup><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\frac{S_{\Delta}\cdot I_{exp_{i}}}{S_{\Delta}\cdot\sum_{j}^{d}I_{exp_{j}}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
